This divergence has produced concrete "wrong answer" bug reports.** SERVER-40232, "$geoIntersects works incorrect" (reported 2019-03-20 against MongoDB 4.0.0, Geo/Querying components, closed as *Done*): a user's two visually-overlapping GeoJSON polygons consistently returned no intersection. The ticket's attached diagram is named `no-intersection-with-great-arcs.png` — i.e. under great-arc edges the polygons genuinely do not overlap, and the behaviour is not a code defect.

The announcement names "polygon intersections", GeoJSON support, and "a more accurate spherical model" as the geospatial content of the release. — mongodb.com press release, 19 March 2013 3. `$geoIntersects` arrived as part of a bundle: MongoDB 2

This report covers only the MongoDB query operator `$geoIntersects`: what it means, how the server decides a match, which parts of the stack it depends on, the invariants it assumes about input geometry, and where it stops working. Sibling operators (`$geoWithin`, `$near`, `$nearSphere`, `$geoNear`) appear only where they are needed to fix the boundary of `$geoIntersects` itself. The 2dsphere index and the S2 library are treated as dependencies, described only to the depth needed to explain how `$geoIntersects` is evaluated — they are separate frontier items.

Atlas / MongoDB Search offers `geoShape`, which supports four relations — `contains`, `disjoint`, `intersects`, `within` — against a field indexed as `geo` with `indexShapes: true`. `intersects` is the direct analogue of `$geoIntersects`, and `disjoint` has no query-language equivalent. ([MongoDB Atlas — geoShape operator](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-search/operators-collectors/geoshape/))

**25.** Multi-geometries (MultiPoint, MultiLineString, MultiPolygon) and GeometryCollection are evaluated componentwise: the container iterates members and returns true if **any one** intersects. Mechanically, this is why `$geoIntersects` is disjunctive over multi-part geometry — a document need not intersect every part. **S1** `[M20, M21 [inf]]` — same file

14. Under the default CRS, a query geometry with an area greater than a single hemisphere causes `$geoIntersects` to query the *complementary* geometry — the smaller of the two regions the ring divides the sphere into. A query polygon covering 75% of Earth's surface returns documents from the other 25%. ([MongoDB Manual v8.0](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/v8.0/reference/operator/query/geointersects/))

**62.** `$geoIntersects` degrades sharply against high-vertex-count **stored** geometries, and the index does not help. Explain shows near-identical IXSCAN work in both cases (239–241 keys, 233–234 documents examined). **S2**

38. Under the default CRS, a query geometry larger than one hemisphere is silently reinterpreted as its complement: "If a specified geometry covers more than a hemisphere, the default CRS query returns documents for the complementary geometry." A geometry covering 75% of Earth's surface is queried as the remaining 25%. — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/geoIntersects/

**E1. Self-intersecting polygons cannot be indexed, so they are unqueryable.** "For Polygons with a single ring, the ring cannot self-intersect"; "The exterior ring cannot self-intersect"; "Interior rings cannot intersect or overlap each other. Interior rings cannot share an edge." Independently: MongoDB "does not support self-intersecting polygons" — you can store them, but "geospatial query operators can't search through them and your 2dsphere index builds will fail." Self-intersections are noted as common in US ZIP-code datasets. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/geojso

It deliberately does **not** cover sibling operators (`$geoWithin`, `$near`, `$nearSphere`, `$geoNear`), the 2dsphere index as a topic in its own right, or GeoJSON storage in general. Those appear here only where they are load-bearing for a `$geoIntersects` failure mode.

**A1. Only the 2dsphere index supports `$geoIntersects`; the 2d index does not.** MongoDB states: "Only the 2dsphere geospatial index supports `$geoIntersects`." A 2d index cannot serve the operator, so a collection indexed only with `2d` silently falls back to a collection scan or errors depending on the query shape.

**A2. `$geoIntersects` does not require any geospatial index.** "$geoIntersects does not require a geospatial index. However, a geospatial index will improve query performance." This is a correctness trap in reverse: an unindexed `$geoIntersects` query returns correct results but performs a full collection scan, so a dropped or failed index build degrades latency without producing an error.

**B1. MongoDB explicitly disclaims boundary-only intersection.** The operator reference states: "$geoIntersects does not guarantee that it will consider a polygon to intersect with its own edges; its own vertices; or another polygon sharing vertices or edges but no interior space." This is the single most important correctness caveat: two polygons that share only a border — adjacent administrative regions, tiled grid cells, a route running exactly along a boundary — may or may not match, and the behaviour is not contractual.

**D4. The strict-winding CRS is query-only; you cannot store a big polygon.** SERVER-45189, "Allow strictwinding property also for inserted geometries (or support geojson standard rfc7946)" (created 2019-12-17, status **Backlog / unresolved**): the CRS is accepted only by query operators such as `$geoWithin` and `$geoIntersects`, not on insert, so polygons exceeding 180° cannot be stored unambiguously — inserted without the CRS, MongoDB interprets them as the opposite hemisphere. Related open tickets: SERVER-15388, SERVER-47651. Practical consequence: `$geoIntersects` can *query with* a big po

Sibling operators (`$geoWithin`, `$near`, `$nearSphere`, `$geoNear`) and the wider MongoDB geospatial domain appear only where a stated `$geoIntersects` behaviour is defined by contrast with them. **Corroborating context, not resolution:** `[M45]` notes the internal tests are named `MayIntersect`, an S2 predicate that is conservative over cells rather than exact — a plausible but explicitly unconfirmed mechanical origin for the hedge. `[H14]` notes that under OGC `Intersects`, boundary-only contact *is* an intersection, so Side A is where MongoDB departs from the predicate it is named for. `[P27]` notes PostGIS `geography` resolves the same ambiguity with an explicit 0.00001 m tolerance, which MongoDB does not expose.

**A4. `$geometry` is mandatory under `$geoIntersects`, unlike some sibling operators.** An independent 2016 write-up notes the `$geometry` property "is required under `$geoIntersects`, though not for other geospatial operators" — `$geoWithin` accepts shorthand forms such as `$box`, `$center`, `$polygon` that `$geoIntersects` does not. Source: https://thecodebarbarian.com/80-20-guide-to-mongodb-geospatial-queries (2016-10-14)

**C1. MongoDB evaluates `$geoIntersects` on a sphere using WGS84, treating edges as geodesics.** "MongoDB geospatial queries on GeoJSON objects calculate on a sphere; MongoDB uses the WGS84 reference system." The GeoJSON page warns: "Lines between two points on a curved surface, or geodesics, can differ from lines between the same points on a flat surface. Check coordinates carefully to avoid shared-edge errors, overlaps, or other intersections."

**E2. The failure surfaces as an index-build error naming the crossing edges.** Verbatim from a 2023 community report: `"errmsg" : "Index build failed: ... Can't extract geo keys: [long error document suppressed] Edges 15 and 35 cross. Edge locations in degrees: [-53.0000000, 119.3750000]-[-52.0000000, 119.3750000] and [-60.0000000, 119.3750000]-[-60.5000000, 119.3750000]"` One bad document blocks the whole index build, and with no index `$geoIntersects` reverts to a collection scan (A2) rather than failing loudly.

**G2. Time-series collections restrict geospatial querying.** "Time series collections only support the `$geoNear` aggregation stage for sorting geospatial data from queries against 2dsphere indexes. You can't use `$near` and `$nearSphere` operators on time series collections." The manual does not list `$geoIntersects` among the prohibited operators; treat its behaviour on time-series collections as unverified rather than supported.

**G3. Point-vs-polygon is the one case where `$geoIntersects` and `$geoWithin` are interchangeable.** "For point-in-polygon queries, $geoIntersects and $geoWithin produce equivalent results." They diverge for polygon-vs-polygon, where `$geoIntersects` matches partial overlap and `$geoWithin` requires complete containment. Note that this equivalence claim is from a secondary source and sits uneasily beside B1 for points lying exactly on a boundary. Source: https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-03-31-mongodb-how-to-use-geointersects-for-overlapping-geometries-in-mongo/view (2026-03-31)

**A. Geodesic vs. Cartesian edges — a direct conflict with the format's own spec.** RFC 7946 states that "A line between two positions is a straight Cartesian line, the shortest line between those two points in the coordinate reference system", and warns "Note that this line may markedly differ from the geodesic path along the curved surface of the reference ellipsoid" (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7946). MongoDB interprets the same GeoJSON edges as geodesics on a sphere (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/geojson/). Both are primary sources and they disagree about what

6. `$geoIntersects` differs from `$geoWithin` in strictness: `$geoWithin` returns only geometries contained entirely within the query geometry, while `$geoIntersects` returns any geometry that overlaps at all, including partial overlaps and full containment. For stored Point data the two return the same result; the difference appears once stored documents hold polygons or lines. ([thecodebarbarian.com, 2016-10-14](https://thecodebarbarian.com/80-20-guide-to-mongodb-geospatial-queries))

21. `$geoIntersects` performance degrades sharply on stored polygons with very many vertices. In SERVER-20843 (reported against 3.0.6), adding a single ~130,000-point polygon to a collection of 9,999 smaller polygons moved query time from ~1 ms to ~87 ms while returning only one extra document. Explain output showed near-identical index scan work in both cases (IXSCAN examining 239–241 keys, 233–234 documents), placing the cost in the post-index geometry filtering stage rather than the index. ([SERVER-20843](https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-20843))

27. PostGIS separates the two geometry models explicitly: the `geometry` type computes planar Cartesian relationships and the `geography` type computes geodesic ones on the spheroid, and `ST_Intersects` on `geography` applies a 0.00001 m tolerance so very close points count as intersecting. MongoDB offers no such tolerance knob and no planar mode for `$geoIntersects`, which is why boundary-contact behaviour is left undefined rather than configurable (claim 18). ([PostGIS — ST_Intersects](https://postgis.net/docs/ST_Intersects.html); [PostGIS — geography introduction](http://postgis.net/worksho

([MongoDB Manual](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/geoIntersects/))

**Consequence:** the same GeoJSON document denotes two different regions. A polygon spanning large longitudes encloses a materially different area in MongoDB than in a conformant reader, so `$geoIntersects` results are **not portable across GeoJSON implementations**. The gap is unbounded for wide or high-latitude rings, was the root cause in SERVER-40232 (claim 51), and is the documented source of Turf-vs-MongoDB disagreement (claim 52). The escape hatch is the custom CRS `urn:x-mongodb:crs:strictwinding:EPSG:4326`, added in MongoDB 3.0.** Under this CRS the queried area is the one "on the left hand side of the direction of points" — counter-clockwise winding selects the interior, matching KML and WKT/WKB conventions. It appears as a sibling of `type` and `coordinates` inside `$geometry`. It is only meaningful for areas at or above a hemisphere; below that its behaviour is documented as identical to the default CRS.
